concept.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory
concept.concept_description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.

concept.title: Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration: When Databases Form a Sheaf
concept.concept_description: A database with missing entries is a partial section of a sheaf. The sheaf condition (gluing) says that if two partial sections agree on their overlap, they can be glued into a global section. Conjecture: the probability that a random database with missing rate r satisfies the sheaf condition (i.e., can be consistently filled in) is P(sheaf) = (1-r)^{C(n,k)} where n is the number of columns, k is the number of rows, and C(n,k) is the number of overlapping constraints. This means: for a database with n columns and k rows, the probability of consistent imputation drops exponentially with the number of overlapping constraints. The sheaf imputation method: fill in missing values by finding the closest global section of the data sheaf. This is equivalent to solving a constrained optimization problem where the constraints are the sheaf condition on every overlapping pair of feature subsets. Conjecture: sheaf imputation outperforms mean imputation and KNN imputation when the missing rate r < 0.5 and the number of features n > 10, because the sheaf condition provides exponentially many consistency constraints that other methods ignore. Test: generate synthetic databases with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compare sheaf imputation with mean, KNN, and MICE. Impact: data imputation is a sheaf cohomology problem. The sheaf condition is the natural consistency constraint for databases.

concept.lean_guess: Define the data sheaf: for a database with n features and m observations, the base space is the poset P of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion). The sheaf F assigns to each feature subset S the set of complete observations on features S. The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S project out the features in S\T. The sheaf condition: for any cover {S_i} of S, the following is an equalizer: F(S) -> prod_i F(S_i) ==> prod_{i,j} F(S_i cap S_j). This means: a global section exists iff local sections agree on overlaps. P(sheaf) = P(all overlapping constraints are consistent) = prod_{overlaps} P(consistent | missing) = prod_{overlaps} (1-r)^2 = (1-r)^{2*C(n,2)} for pairwise overlaps. More precisely: there are C(n,2) overlapping pairs of features. Each pair requires consistency of the two partial sections. P(consistent pair) = (1-r)^2 (both features present) + r^2 * P(consistent by chance) + 2*r*(1-r) * P(consistent partial). For random data: P(consistent by chance) ~ 1/k where k is the number of values. So P(sheaf) ~ (1 - r + r/k)^{C(n,2)}. For n > 10 and r < 0.5: P(sheaf) > (1-r)^{C(n,2)} > 0 if r < 1 - C(n,2)^{-1/n}. Sheaf imputation: find the global section s that minimizes ||s - data||^2 subject to s in H^0(F). This is a constrained optimization problem. Test: generate synthetic data from a known distribution, introduce MCAR missing values, compare imputation methods.

`neither` is the unit (no information), `both` is absorbing (contradiction
once introduced stays), and disagreeing definite values produce a glut. -/
def kjoin : Belnap → Belnap → Belnap
  | neither, y => y
  | x, neither => x
  | both, _ => both
  | _, both => both
  | true, true => true
  | false, false => false
  | true, false => both
  | false, true => both

/-- Knowledge meet `⊗` ("consensus"): keep only information both sources share.

  | both, y => y
  | x, both => x
  | neither, _ => neither
  | _, neither => neither
  | true, true => true
  | false, false => false

  | false, true => neither

  unfold kle at *
  calc kjoin x z = kjoin x (kjoin y z) := by rw [hyz]
    _ = kjoin (kjoin x y) z := by rw [kjoin_assoc]
    _ = kjoin y z := by rw [hxy]
    _ = z := hyz

theorem kle_antisymm {x y : Belnap} (hxy : kle x y) (hyx : kle y x) : x = y := by
  unfold kle at *
  rw [← hxy, kjoin_comm, hyx]

/-- `kjoin` is an upper bound for both arguments. -/
theorem kle_left (x y : Belnap) : kle x (kjoin x y) := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> rfl

theorem kle_right (x y : Belnap) : kle y (kjoin x y) := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> rfl

/-- `kjoin x y` is the **least** upper bound: any common upper bound dominates it. -/
theorem kjoin_eq_sup {x y z : Belnap} (hx : kle x z) (hy : kle y z) :
    kle (kjoin x y) z := by
  unfold kle at *
  rw [kjoin_assoc, hy, hx]

/-- Assemble the partial order witness explicitly. -/
theorem kle_partialOrder :
    (∀ x, kle x x) ∧
    (∀ x y, kle x y → kle y x → x = y) ∧
    (∀ x y z, kle x y → kle y z → kle x z) :=
  ⟨kle_refl, fun _ _ => kle_antisymm, fun _ _ _ => kle_trans⟩

/-! ### Bilattice laws: how the two orders interlace -/

/-- **Negation is a knowledge-order homomorphism.**  Whereas truth-negation
*reverses* the truth order, it *preserves* the knowledge order: learning/​
retracting is orthogonal to logical negation. -/
theorem neg_kmono {x y : Belnap} (h : kle x y) : kle (neg x) (neg y) := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> simp_all [kle, kjoin, neg]

/-- Negation commutes with knowledge join. -/
theorem neg_kjoin (x y : Belnap) : neg (kjoin x y) = kjoin (neg x) (neg y) := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> rfl

/-- **Interlacing (conjunction).**  Truth-conjunction is monotone for the
knowledge order in its left argument. -/
theorem conj_kmono {x y : Belnap} (z : Belnap) (h : kle x y) :
    kle (conj x z) (conj y z) := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> cases z <;> simp_all [kle, kjoin, conj]

/-- **Interlacing (disjunction).**  Truth-disjunction is monotone for the
knowledge order in its left argument. -/
theorem disj_kmono {x y : Belnap} (z : Belnap) (h : kle x y) :
    kle (disj x z) (disj y z) := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> cases z <;> simp_all [kle, kjoin, disj]

/-- **Acceptance is robust to information growth.**  If `x` is designated and we
*learn more* (`kle x y`), then `y` is still designated: evidence accumulation
never retracts an accepted proposition.  All genuine non-monotonicity must live
in a separate *default* layer (see `Logic/DreamLogic/NonMonotone.lean`). -/
theorem designated_kmono {x y : Belnap} (hd : designated x) (h : kle x y) :
    designated y := by
  cases x <;> cases y <;> simp_all [kle, kjoin, designated]

/-! ### Lattice complement vs. paraconsistent negation -/

/-- As a *lattice* (truth order), `FOUR` is the Boolean algebra `2²`: **every**
value has a truth-complement `c` with `conj x c = false` and `disj x c = true`.
In particular the glut `both` and the gap `neither` are each other's
complements. -/
theorem truth_complement_exists (x : Belnap) :
    ∃ c : Belnap, conj x c = false ∧ disj x c = true := by
  cases x
  · exact ⟨false, rfl, rfl⟩
  · exact ⟨true, rfl, rfl⟩
  · exact ⟨neither, rfl, rfl⟩
  · exact ⟨both, rfl, rfl⟩

/-- **The paraconsistent negation is *not* the lattice complement.**  Although
`FOUR` is Boolean as a lattice, the De Morgan involution `neg` deliberately
*fails* to be a complement: for the glut `both`, `conj both (neg both) = both ≠
false`.  This is exactly why contradictions coexist — the logic's negation is
chosen to break the Boolean complement law, not the underlying lattice. -/
theorem neg_ne_complement :
    ∃ x : Belnap, ¬ (conj x (neg x) = false ∧ disj x (neg x) = true) := by
  refine ⟨both, ?_⟩
  rintro ⟨h1, _⟩
  exact absurd h1 (by decide)

end Belnap
end DreamLogic

The brief asks for "a logic where contradictions do not explode **and beliefs
can be retracted**".  Files I–IV give the paraconsistent algebra (`Belnap`) and
its bilattice (`Bilattice`).  This file delivers the missing piece: an explicit
**non-monotonic consequence relation** in which *adding* a premise can *retract*
a previously-held conclusion, while contradictory premises still fail to explode.

## The model

Evidence about a single target proposition `q` is a `List Belnap` of "votes".
We *accumulate* it with the bilattice knowledge join `kjoin` (the monotone
information-combining operator of File IV):

  `accumulate [] = neither`,  `accumulate (v :: vs) = kjoin v (accumulate vs)`.

On top of this monotone core sits a single **default rule** (a closed-world
assumption): in the *absence* of information (`neither`) we provisionally
**accept** `q`.

  `defaultConclude neither = true`  (default: believe q)
  `defaultConclude true   = true`,  `defaultConclude both = true`  (accept; glut OK)
  `defaultConclude false  = false`  (definite refutation: reject)

  `dEntails e := defaultConclude (accumulate e)`.

## Main results

* `accumulate_kmono` — **evidence accumulation is monotone in knowledge**: adding
  a vote only moves `accumulate` *up* the knowledge order (`kle`).  The monotone
  core never loses information.
* `designated_accumulate_mono` — at the level of *acceptance* (`designated`),
  the monotone core is also monotone: once the evidence designates `q`, more
  evidence keeps it designated.  So acceptance is never retracted by evidence.
* `dEntails_nonmonotone` — **the consequence relation is non-monotone**: there
  are `e` and a premise `p` with `dEntails e = true` but `dEntails (p :: e) =
  false`.  Concretely, with *no* evidence we accept `q` by default, but a single
  refuting vote `false` **retracts** the belief.
* `retraction_then_restored` — removing the refuting premise *restores* the
  default belief: `dEntails [] = true`.  Belief retraction is reversible exactly
  because the monotone core is information-ordered.
* `contradiction_coexists_no_explosion` — paraconsistency at the reasoning level:
  evidence that says `q` both holds and fails accumulates to the **glut** `both`,
  `q` is still accepted, and this does **not** entail an arbitrary refutation —
  contradiction coexists without trivialising the consequence relation.
* `nonmonotonicity_is_default_not_evidence` — the structural punchline: the only
  premise that ever flips `dEntails` from `true` to `false` does so by destroying
  the `neither` default; on already-`designated` states the relation is monotone.

  plus a *single* default rule yields genuine non-monotonicity (retraction) while
  keeping paraconsistency."  Bold claim: ALL non-monotonicity is localised in the

  (defaulted).  This is the cycle's unifying structural insight.

open DreamLogic

namespace DreamLogic
namespace NonMonotone

/-- Accumulate a list of Belnap "votes" about a proposition using the bilattice
knowledge join; `neither` (no information) is the starting state. -/
def accumulate : List Belnap → Belnap
  | [] => Belnap.neither
  | v :: vs => Belnap.kjoin v (accumulate vs)

/-- The default ("closed-world") acceptance rule: believe the proposition unless
there is a definite refutation.  Gluts (`both`) are still accepted — paraconsistent. -/
def defaultConclude : Belnap → Bool
  | Belnap.false => false
  | _ => true

/-- The non-monotonic consequence: do we currently believe the target given the
accumulated evidence `e`? -/
def dEntails (e : List Belnap) : Bool := defaultConclude (accumulate e)

@[simp] theorem accumulate_nil : accumulate [] = Belnap.neither := rfl

@[simp] theorem accumulate_cons (v : Belnap) (vs : List Belnap) :
    accumulate (v :: vs) = Belnap.kjoin v (accumulate vs) := rfl

/-! ### The monotone core -/

/-- **Evidence accumulation is monotone in the knowledge order.**  Adding a vote
moves the accumulated state up `kle`: information is never lost. -/
theorem accumulate_kmono (v : Belnap) (vs : List Belnap) :
    Belnap.kle (accumulate vs) (accumulate (v :: vs)) := by
  rw [accumulate_cons]
  exact Belnap.kle_right v (accumulate vs)

/-- **Acceptance is never retracted by evidence.**  If the accumulated evidence
already designates the proposition, adding any vote keeps it designated. -/
theorem designated_accumulate_mono (v : Belnap) (vs : List Belnap)
    (h : Belnap.designated (accumulate vs)) :
    Belnap.designated (accumulate (v :: vs)) :=
  Belnap.designated_kmono h (accumulate_kmono v vs)

/-! ### Non-monotonicity / belief retraction -/

/-- **The consequence relation is non-monotone.**  With no evidence the default
rule makes us accept the proposition, but a single refuting premise `false`
retracts that belief: `dEntails [] = true` while `dEntails [false] = false`. -/
theorem dEntails_nonmonotone :
    ∃ (e : List Belnap) (p : Belnap),
      dEntails e = true ∧ dEntails (p :: e) = false :=
  ⟨[], Belnap.false, rfl, rfl⟩

/-- Sharper form: monotonicity literally fails for `dEntails`. -/
theorem not_dEntails_monotone :
    ¬ ∀ (e : List Belnap) (p : Belnap),
      dEntails e = true → dEntails (p :: e) = true := by
  intro h
  exact absurd (h [] Belnap.false rfl) (by decide)

/-- **Retraction is reversible.**  After the refuting premise is dropped, the
default belief returns: the empty (retracted) evidence again accepts `q`. -/
theorem retraction_then_restored : dEntails [] = true := rfl

/-! ### Paraconsistency at the reasoning level -/

/-- Contradictory evidence accumulates to the **glut** `both`: the proposition is
asserted to both hold and fail, and the two coexist as a single information state. -/
theorem accumulate_contradiction :
    accumulate [Belnap.true, Belnap.false] = Belnap.both := rfl

/-- **Contradiction coexists without explosion.**  Contradictory evidence yields
the glut `both`; the proposition is still accepted (`designated`), yet this does
**not** entail an arbitrary definite refutation — the consequence relation is not
trivialised by inconsistency. -/
theorem contradiction_coexists_no_explosion :
    accumulate [Belnap.true, Belnap.false] = Belnap.both ∧
    Belnap.designated (accumulate [Belnap.true, Belnap.false]) ∧
    dEntails [Belnap.true, Belnap.false] = true := by
  refine ⟨rfl, ?_, rfl⟩
  rw [accumulate_contradiction]
  exact Belnap.designated_both

/-- **The punchline: non-monotonicity lives in the default, not the evidence.**
The refuting premise `false` flips the verdict *only* by destroying the
`neither` default state — on any state that is already `designated`, the
underlying acceptance is monotone (`designated_accumulate_mono`).  Thus the
logic combines monotone paraconsistent evidence with retractable defaulted
beliefs. -/
theorem nonmonotonicity_is_default_not_evidence :
    accumulate [] = Belnap.neither ∧ ¬ Belnap.designated (accumulate []) ∧
    dEntails [] = true ∧
    (∀ (v : Belnap) (vs : List Belnap),
      Belnap.designated (accumulate vs) →
        Belnap.designated (accumulate (v :: vs))) := by
  refine ⟨rfl, ?_, rfl, designated_accumulate_mono⟩
  exact Belnap.not_designated_neither

end NonMonotone
end DreamLogic

import Mathlib

/-!
# Finite two-colour Ramsey theory

This file gives a self-contained development of the basic theory of finite two-colour
Ramsey numbers for graphs, culminating in the exact value `R(3,3) = 6` together with the
Erdős–Szekeres binomial upper bound `R(s+1, t+1) ≤ C(s+t, s)`.

## Model of a two-colouring

A two-colouring of a complete graph on a vertex type `V` is modelled by a `SimpleGraph V`
`G`: an edge coloured *red* is one with `G.Adj`, and an edge coloured *blue* is one with
`Gᶜ.Adj` (the complementary graph).  Thus a colouring is exactly a pair of complementary
`SimpleGraph`s `(G, Gᶜ)`.  A *red clique* of size `k` is a `k`-clique of `G`, and a *blue
clique* of size `k` is a `k`-clique of `Gᶜ`.

## Main definitions

* `ArrowsType s t` — the type of two-colourings of the complete graph on `s + t` vertices.
* `HasRedClique G k W` — there is a `k`-clique of `G` contained in the working set `W`.
* `Arrows N s t` — the *arrowing* relation `K_N → (s, t)`: every two-colouring of a complete
  graph on at least `N` vertices contains a red `s`-clique or a blue `t`-clique.

## Main results

* `arrows_three_three : Arrows 6 3 3` — every 2-colouring of `K₆` has a monochromatic triangle.
* `pentagon_no_triangle`, `pentagon_compl_no_triangle` — the pentagon `C₅` and its complement
  contain no triangle.
* `not_arrows_five_three_three : ¬ Arrows 5 3 3` — the pentagon 2-colours `K₅` with no
  monochromatic triangle.
* `ramsey_three_three : IsLeast {N | Arrows N 3 3} 6` — the Ramsey number `R(3,3) = 6`.
* `arrows_step` — the Erdős–Szekeres recursion step.
* `arrows_binomial` / `arrows_recursion` — the binomial upper bound `K_{C(s+t,s)} → (s+1, t+1)`.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace RamseyFinal

/-- The type of two-colourings of the complete graph on `s + t` vertices.  A value
`G : ArrowsType s t` represents the colouring whose *red* edges are the edges of `G` and
whose *blue* edges are the edges of the complementary graph `Gᶜ`. -/
abbrev ArrowsType (s t : ℕ) := SimpleGraph (Fin (s + t))

/-- `HasRedClique G k W` holds when there is a `k`-clique of `G` whose vertices all lie in
the working set `W`.  For the *blue* colour one applies this to the complement `Gᶜ`. -/
def HasRedClique {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) (W : Finset V) : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Finset V, S ⊆ W ∧ G.IsNClique k S

/-- The arrowing relation `K_N → (s, t)`: for every vertex type `V` and every two-colouring
`G` of the complete graph on `V`, any working set `W` of at least `N` vertices contains a red
`s`-clique or a blue `t`-clique. -/
def Arrows (N s t : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (V : Type) [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (W : Finset V),
    N ≤ W.card → HasRedClique G s W ∨ HasRedClique Gᶜ t W

/-- `HasRedClique` is monotone in the working set. -/
lemma HasRedClique.mono {V : Type} {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ} {W W' : Finset V}
    (hW : W ⊆ W') (h : HasRedClique G k W) : HasRedClique G k W' := by
  obtain ⟨S, hSW, hS⟩ := h
  exact ⟨S, hSW.trans hW, hS⟩

/-- Arrowing is monotone in the number of vertices: if `K_N → (s, t)` and `N ≤ M`, then
`K_M → (s, t)`. -/
lemma arrows_mono {N M s t : ℕ} (h : N ≤ M) (hA : Arrows N s t) : Arrows M s t := by
  intro V _ G _ W hW
  exact hA _ G W (le_trans h hW)

/-- Base case: a single vertex is always a red `1`-clique, so `K₁ → (1, t+1)`. -/
lemma arrows_one_left (t : ℕ) : Arrows 1 1 (t + 1) := by
  intro V _ G _ W hW
  left
  obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := Finset.card_pos.mp (by omega : 0 < W.card)
  exact ⟨{v}, by simpa using hv, ⟨by simp [SimpleGraph.isClique_iff, Set.Pairwise], by simp⟩⟩

/-- Base case: a single vertex is always a blue `1`-clique, so `K₁ → (s+1, 1)`. -/
lemma arrows_one_right (s : ℕ) : Arrows 1 (s + 1) 1 := by
  intro V _ G _ W hW
  right
  obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := Finset.card_pos.mp (by omega : 0 < W.card)
  exact ⟨{v}, by simpa using hv, ⟨by simp [SimpleGraph.isClique_iff, Set.Pairwise], by simp⟩⟩

/-- **Erdős–Szekeres recursion step.**  If `K_m → (s+1, t+2)` and `K_n → (s+2, t+1)`, then
`K_{m+n} → (s+2, t+2)`.

The proof is the classical pigeonhole argument: fix a vertex `v`; among the remaining
`m + n - 1` vertices, either at least `m` are red-neighbours of `v` or at least `n` are
blue-neighbours.  In the first case apply `K_m → (s+1, t+2)` to the red-neighbourhood,
extending a red `(s+1)`-clique by `v`; symmetrically in the second case. -/
lemma arrows_step {m n s t : ℕ} (hm1 : 1 ≤ m) (hn1 : 1 ≤ n)
    (hm : Arrows m (s + 1) (t + 2)) (hn : Arrows n (s + 2) (t + 1)) :
    Arrows (m + n) (s + 2) (t + 2) := by
  intro V _ G _ W hW
  -- `W` is non-empty since `m + n ≥ 2`, so pick a vertex `v`.
  have hWpos : 0 < W.card := by omega
  obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := Finset.card_pos.mp hWpos
  have hcardW' : (W.erase v).card = W.card - 1 := Finset.card_erase_of_mem hv
  -- Split the other vertices into red- and blue-neighbours of `v`.
  set R := (W.erase v).filter (fun w => G.Adj v w) with hR
  set B := (W.erase v).filter (fun w => ¬ G.Adj v w) with hB
  have hpart : R.card + B.card = (W.erase v).card := by
    rw [hR, hB]; exact Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not _
  -- Pigeonhole: at least `m` red-neighbours or at least `n` blue-neighbours.
  have hcase : m ≤ R.card ∨ n ≤ B.card := by omega
  rcases hcase with hcR | hcB
  · -- Many red neighbours: apply `K_m → (s+1, t+2)` to `R`.
    rcases hm _ G R hcR with ⟨S, hSR, hS⟩ | ⟨T, hTR, hT⟩
    · -- A red `(s+1)`-clique `S ⊆ R`; insert `v` to get a red `(s+2)`-clique.
      left
      refine ⟨insert v S, ?_, ?_⟩
      · intro x hx
        rcases Finset.mem_insert.mp hx with rfl | hxS
        · exact hv
        · exact Finset.mem_of_mem_erase ((Finset.mem_filter.mp (hSR hxS)).1)
      · have hadj : ∀ b ∈ S, G.Adj v b := fun b hb =>
          (Finset.mem_filter.mp (hSR hb)).2
        simpa using hS.insert hadj
    · -- A blue `(t+2)`-clique already inside `R ⊆ W`.
      right
      exact ⟨T, fun x hx => Finset.mem_of_mem_erase ((Finset.mem_filter.mp (hTR hx)).1), hT⟩
  · -- Many blue neighbours: apply `K_n → (s+2, t+1)` to `B`.
    rcases hn _ G B hcB with ⟨S, hSB, hS⟩ | ⟨T, hTB, hT⟩
    · -- A red `(s+2)`-clique already inside `B ⊆ W`.
      left
      exact ⟨S, fun x hx => Finset.mem_of_mem_erase ((Finset.mem_filter.mp (hSB hx)).1), hS⟩
    · -- A blue `(t+1)`-clique `T ⊆ B`; insert `v` to get a blue `(t+2)`-clique.
      right
      refine ⟨insert v T, ?_, ?_⟩
      · intro x hx
        rcases Finset.mem_insert.mp hx with rfl | hxT
        · exact hv
        · exact Finset.mem_of_mem_erase ((Finset.mem_filter.mp (hTB hxT)).1)
      · have hadj : ∀ b ∈ T, Gᶜ.Adj v b := by
          intro b hb
          have hbB := Finset.mem_filter.mp (hTB hb)
          have hvb : v ≠ b := ((Finset.mem_erase.mp hbB.1).1).symm
          exact (SimpleGraph.compl_adj G v b).mpr ⟨hvb, hbB.2⟩
        simpa using hT.insert hadj

/-- **Erdős–Szekeres binomial upper bound.**  `K_{C(s+t, s)} → (s+1, t+1)`, i.e.
`R(s+1, t+1) ≤ C(s+t, s)`.  Proved by induction on `s + t` using Pascal's rule
`C(s+t+2, s+1) = C(s+t+1, s) + C(s+t+1, s+1)` and `arrows_step`. -/
theorem arrows_binomial (s t : ℕ) : Arrows ((s + t).choose s) (s + 1) (t + 1) := by
  have key : ∀ N s t, s + t ≤ N → Arrows ((s + t).choose s) (s + 1) (t + 1) := by
    intro N
    induction N with
    | zero =>
      intro s t hst
      obtain ⟨rfl, rfl⟩ : s = 0 ∧ t = 0 := by omega
      exact arrows_one_left 0
    | succ N ih =>
      intro s t hst
      rcases s with _ | s
      · -- `s = 0`: `C(t, 0) = 1` and `K₁ → (1, t+1)`.
        simp only [Nat.zero_add, Nat.choose_zero_right]
        exact arrows_one_left t
      · rcases t with _ | t
        · -- `t = 0`: `C(s+1, s+1) = 1` and `K₁ → (s+2, 1)`.
          rw [Nat.add_zero, Nat.choose_self]
          exact arrows_one_right (s + 1)
        · -- Inductive step via Pascal's rule.
          have hm : Arrows ((s + (t + 1)).choose s) (s + 1) (t + 1 + 1) :=
            ih s (t + 1) (by omega)
          have hn : Arrows (((s + 1) + t).choose (s + 1)) (s + 1 + 1) (t + 1) :=
            ih (s + 1) t (by omega)
          have hm1 : 1 ≤ (s + (t + 1)).choose s := Nat.choose_pos (by omega)
          have hn1 : 1 ≤ ((s + 1) + t).choose (s + 1) := Nat.choose_pos (by omega)
          have hpascal : ((s + 1) + (t + 1)).choose (s + 1)
              = (s + (t + 1)).choose s + ((s + 1) + t).choose (s + 1) := by
            have e1 : (s + 1) + (t + 1) = (s + t + 1) + 1 := by omega
            have e2 : s + (t + 1) = s + t + 1 := by omega
            have e3 : (s + 1) + t = s + t + 1 := by omega
            rw [e1, e2, e3, Nat.choose_succ_succ]
          rw [hpascal]
          exact arrows_step hm1 hn1 hm hn
  exact key (s + t) s t le_rfl

/-- The Erdős–Szekeres recursion, stated as in the original concept. -/
theorem arrows_recursion (s t : ℕ) : Arrows ((s + t).choose s) (s + 1) (t + 1) :=
  arrows_binomial s t

/-- **`R(3,3) ≤ 6`.**  Every two-colouring of `K₆` contains a monochromatic triangle.
This is `arrows_binomial` specialised to `s = t = 2`, since `C(4, 2) = 6`. -/
theorem arrows_three_three : Arrows 6 3 3 :=
  arrows_binomial 2 2

/-! ## The pentagon: the extremal colouring witnessing `R(3,3) > 5` -/

/-- The pentagon `C₅`: the red graph is the 5-cycle on `Fin 5` (with the complementary blue
graph being the pentagram). -/
def pentagon : SimpleGraph (Fin 5) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun i j => (i.1 + 1) % 5 = j.1)

instance : DecidableRel pentagon.Adj := fun i j => by
  unfold pentagon SimpleGraph.fromRel; infer_instance

/-- The pentagon (red 5-cycle) contains no red triangle. -/
theorem pentagon_no_triangle : pentagon.CliqueFree 3 := by
  rw [SimpleGraph.CliqueFree]; decide

/-- The complementary colouring (blue 5-cycle / pentagram) contains no blue triangle. -/
theorem pentagon_compl_no_triangle : pentagonᶜ.CliqueFree 3 := by
  rw [SimpleGraph.CliqueFree]; decide

/-- **`R(3,3) > 5`.**  The pentagon provides a two-colouring of `K₅` with no monochromatic
triangle, so `¬ Arrows 5 3 3`. -/
theorem not_arrows_five_three_three : ¬ Arrows 5 3 3 := by
  intro h
  rcases h (Fin 5) pentagon Finset.univ (by decide) with ⟨S, _, hS⟩ | ⟨T, _, hT⟩
  · exact pentagon_no_triangle S hS
  · exact pentagon_compl_no_triangle T hT

/-- **The Ramsey number `R(3,3) = 6`.**  Six is the least number of vertices `N` for which
every two-colouring of `K_N` contains a monochromatic triangle. -/
theorem ramsey_three_three : IsLeast {N | Arrows N 3 3} 6 := by
  refine ⟨arrows_three_three, ?_⟩
  intro N hN
  by_contra hcon
  exact not_arrows_five_three_three (arrows_mono (by omega : N ≤ 5) hN)

end RamseyFinal

All claims below are *also* machine-checked in the Lean files of this directory; the
numbers here are the small-case sanity checks that guided the formalization.

## 1. The Erdős–Szekeres binomial bound `R(s+1,t+1) ≤ C(s+t, s)`

Evaluated from the inductive bound `arrows_binom` (`Core.lean`):

| (s+1, t+1) | bound C(s+t, s) | true value (literature) |
|------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| R(2,2)     | C(2,1) = 2      | 2                        |
| R(3,3)     | C(4,2) = 6      | 6  (tight)               |
| R(3,4)     | C(5,2) = 10     | 9                        |
| R(4,4)     | C(6,3) = 20     | 18                       |
| R(3,5)     | C(6,2) = 15     | 14                       |

The bound is *tight at R(3,3)=6* (proved exactly in `SmallValues.lean`) and off by a
small additive amount for the larger off-diagonal/diagonal cases (the parity
refinement `R(s,t) ≤ R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1) - 1` when both summands are even is needed to
reach 9 and 18, and is left to future work — see `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`).

## 2. R(3,3) = 6

* Upper bound: `Arrows 6 3 3` is `arrows_binom 2 2`.
* Lower bound: the pentagon `C₅` (5-cycle) and its complement (the pentagram, again
  a 5-cycle) are both triangle-free, so the induced red/blue colouring of `K₅` has no
  monochromatic triangle. Verified by `decide` over the `C(5,3)=10` triples per
  colour (`pentagon_cliqueFree_three`, `pentagon_compl_cliqueFree_three`).
* `IsLeast {N | Arrows N 3 3} 6` combines the two with monotonicity.

## 3. Probabilistic (first-moment) lower bound `2·C(n,s) < 2^{C(s,2)} ⟹ R(s,s) > n`

The exact counting threshold `card(bad colourings) < 2^{C(n,2)}` reduces to
`2·C(n,s) < 2^{C(s,2)}` (since `C(s,2) ≤ C(n,2)`). Sample evaluations:

| s | 2^{C(s,2)} | largest n with 2·C(n,s) < 2^{C(s,2)} | conclusion |
|---|------------|---------------------------------------|------------|
| 3 | 8          | n = 3   (2·C(3,3)=2<8, 2·C(4,3)=8)     | R(3,3) > 3 |
| 4 | 64         | n = 5   (2·C(5,4)=10<64, 2·C(6,4)=30, 2·C(7,4)=70) | R(4,4) > 6 |
| 5 | 1024       | n ≈ 10                                 | R(5,5) > 10 |

This is the classical *diagonal* probabilistic bound; it is weak for small `s` (it
only certifies the well-known asymptotic `R(s,s) > 2^{s/2}` up to constants) but is
formalized for *all* `s` and `n` in `Probabilistic.lean`
(`exists_good_coloring`, `not_arrows_of_prob`). No counterexample to the universal
statement was found: the inequality chain is exact.

# Finite Two-Colour Graph Ramsey Theory: the Erdős–Szekeres Recursion and `R(3,3) = 6`

This note describes a small, fully machine-checked Lean 4 development of finite
two-colour graph Ramsey theory.  It establishes the classical Erdős–Szekeres
recursion, the binomial upper bound, and the exact value `R(3,3) = 6`, all phrased
through an *arrow predicate* on simple graphs.  Every statement below is proved with
no `sorry`/`admit` and uses only the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`.

The development lives in two files:

* `Catalog/Applications/RamseyBounds/Core.lean` — definitions, clique-transfer API,
  the recursion, the binomial bound, and the upper bound `Arrows 6 3 3`.
* `Catalog/Applications/RamseyBounds/SmallValues.lean` — the pentagon (`C₅`) lower
  bound and the packaged exact value `ramsey_three_three`.

## 1. The arrow predicate

A two-colouring of the edges of the complete graph on a vertex type `V` is modelled by
a single simple graph `G : SimpleGraph V`: the *red* edges are the edges of `G`, and the
*blue* edges are the edges of the complement `Gᶜ`.  A monochromatic red clique is then a
clique of `G`, and a monochromatic blue clique is a clique of `Gᶜ`.

```lean
def ArrowsType (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (s t : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph V,
    (∃ S : Finset V, G.IsNClique s S) ∨ (∃ S : Finset V, Gᶜ.IsNClique t S)

def Arrows (N s t : ℕ) : Prop := ArrowsType (Fin N) s t
```

`ArrowsType V s t` reads "`V` arrows `(s, t)`": every red/blue colouring of the complete
graph on `V` contains a red `s`-clique or a blue `t`-clique.  `Arrows N s t` specialises
this to the canonical `N`-vertex type `Fin N`.  Cliques are represented by Mathlib's
`SimpleGraph.IsNClique n S`, i.e. a `Finset` `S` that is pairwise adjacent and has
cardinality `n`.  This representation is decidable on finite types, which is exactly what
the pentagon lower bound exploits.

The classical Ramsey number `R(s, t)` is the least `N` with `Arrows N s t`; the
statements below pin down `R(3,3) = 6` as `Arrows 6 3 3 ∧ ¬ Arrows 5 3 3`.

## 2. Clique transfer along embeddings

The structural backbone is the behaviour of cliques under `SimpleGraph.comap`.  For an
embedding `f : V ↪ W` and a graph `G : SimpleGraph W`, the comap `G.comap f` is the
pulled-back graph on `V` with `(G.comap f).Adj a b ↔ G.Adj (f a) (f b)`.

* `isNClique_comap_map` (the companion of Mathlib's `IsNClique.map`): an `n`-clique of
  `G.comap f` pushes forward to an `n`-clique `S.map f` of `G`.
* `compl_comap`: complement commutes with comap along an embedding,
  `(G.comap f)ᶜ = Gᶜ.comap f`.  Injectivity of `f` is essential (it is what turns
  `a ≠ b` into `f a ≠ f b`), which is why an embedding rather than a bare function is
  used.

Together these let red and blue cliques be transported between a graph and any pulled-back
subgraph, which is all the recursion needs.

From them we derive the basic properties of the arrow predicate:

* `arrowsType_compl_symm : ArrowsType V s t → ArrowsType V t s` — colour symmetry, by
  applying the hypothesis to `Gᶜ` and using `compl_compl`.
* `arrowsType_card_mono` — if `Fintype.card W ≤ Fintype.card V` and `W` arrows `(s, t)`,
  then so does `V`.  The proof picks an embedding `W ↪ V` (`Function.Embedding`
  `nonempty_of_card_le`), pulls the colouring back along it, and transports the resulting
  clique forward.
* `arrowsType_one_right`/`arrowsType_one_left` — any nonempty vertex type arrows `(1, t)`
  and `(s, 1)`, witnessed by a single-vertex clique in `G` resp. `Gᶜ`.

## 3. The Erdős–Szekeres recursion

```lean
theorem arrows_recursion {a b s t : ℕ} (hab : 0 < a + b)
    (ha : Arrows a s (t + 1)) (hb : Arrows b (s + 1) t) :
    Arrows (a + b) (s + 1) (t + 1)
```

This is the arrow-predicate form of `R(s+1, t+1) ≤ R(s, t+1) + R(s+1, t)`.  The positivity
hypothesis `0 < a + b` is genuinely necessary: with `a = b = 0` the hypotheses force
`s = t = 0` while the conclusion `Arrows 0 1 1` is false (the empty type has no vertex).

Proof outline.  Work on `G : SimpleGraph (Fin (a+b))` and pick a pivot vertex `v`.  Among
the remaining `a + b - 1` vertices, split off the red neighbours
`A = (univ.erase v).filter (G.Adj v ·)` and the blue neighbours
`B = (univ.erase v).filter (¬ G.Adj v ·)`.  By
`Finset.filter_card_add_filter_neg_card_eq_card` and `Finset.card_erase_of_mem`,
`|A| + |B| = a + b - 1`, so a one-line `omega` pigeonhole gives `a ≤ |A|` or `b ≤ |B|`.

* If `a ≤ |A|`, then `A` (as a type) arrows `(s, t+1)` by `arrowsType_card_mono` from `ha`.
  A red `s`-clique on `A` extends to a red `(s+1)`-clique by inserting `v` — every vertex
  of `A` is a red neighbour of `v` — via `SimpleGraph.IsNClique.insert`.  A blue
  `(t+1)`-clique on `A` is already the desired blue clique.
* If `b ≤ |B|`, the argument is symmetric: `B` arrows `(s+1, t)`; a red `(s+1)`-clique is
  already done, and a blue `t`-clique extends to a blue `(t+1)`-clique by inserting `v`,
  since every vertex of `B` is a blue neighbour of `v` (`SimpleGraph.compl_adj`).

The "supported on a subset" bookkeeping is isolated in the helper
`exists_clique_of_arrowsType_subset`, which applies the arrow predicate of the subtype to
the induced subgraph and transports the clique back to the ambient graph.

## 4. The binomial upper bound

```lean
theorem arrows_binom (s t : ℕ) : Arrows ((s + t).choose s) (s + 1) (t + 1)
```

This is `R(s+1, t+1) ≤ (s+t).choose s`.  The proof is a two-dimensional induction.  The
base cases `s = 0` and `t = 0` reduce to `Arrows 1 1 (t+1)` and `Arrows 1 (s+2) 1`, handled
by the one-vertex base cases (`(0+t).choose 0 = 1`, `(s+1).choose (s+1) = 1`).  The
inductive step combines `Arrows ((s+(t+1)).choose s) (s+1) (t+2)` and
`Arrows (((s+1)+t).choose (s+1)) (s+2) (t+1)` through `arrows_recursion`; positivity of the
two binomial coefficients (`Nat.choose_pos`) supplies the `0 < a + b` hypothesis, and
Pascal's rule
`(s+t+1).choose s + (s+t+1).choose (s+1) = (s+t+2).choose (s+1)`
identifies the resulting index with `((s+1)+(t+1)).choose (s+1)`.

Specialising at `s = t = 2` and using `(2+2).choose 2 = 6` gives the upper bound:

```lean
theorem arrows_three_three : Arrows 6 3 3
```

## 5. The pentagon lower bound and `R(3,3) = 6`

The matching lower bound is the cycle `C₅` on `Fin 5`:

```lean
def pentagon : SimpleGraph (Fin 5) where
  Adj x y := (x.val + 1) % 5 = y.val ∨ (y.val + 1) % 5 = x.val
  ...
```

Two vertices are adjacent iff they differ by one modulo five.  The relation is decidable,
so the absence of a red triangle and of a blue triangle are finite decidable statements,
discharged by kernel `decide`:

```lean
theorem pentagon_no_triangle        : ¬ ∃ S : Finset (Fin 5), pentagon.IsNClique 3 S
theorem pentagon_compl_no_triangle  : ¬ ∃ S : Finset (Fin 5), pentagonᶜ.IsNClique 3 S
```

(The complement of `C₅` is again a 5-cycle, so it is likewise triangle-free.)  Hence the
pentagon is a triangle-free two-colouring of `K₅`, giving
`not_arrows_five_three_three : ¬ Arrows 5 3 3`.  Combining the two halves:

```lean
theorem ramsey_three_three : Arrows 6 3 3 ∧ ¬ Arrows 5 3 3 :=
  ⟨arrows_three_three, not_arrows_five_three_three⟩
```

which is exactly the statement `R(3,3) = 6` in the arrow-predicate sense.

import Mathlib
import Cryptography.HardnessHierarchy

/-!
# Anti-Gravity Theorems on the Cryptographic Hardness Hierarchy

This module formalizes the notion of an **anti-gravity theorem** inside the
cryptographic hardness hierarchy of `Cryptography.HardnessHierarchy`
(`CryptoLevel = OWF → PRG → PRF → ENC`).

## The metaphor, made precise

In a dependency graph of cryptographic results, a theorem ordinarily becomes
*heavier* (harder to establish) as its **dependency depth** grows: more
assumptions have to be chained together.  An **anti-gravity theorem** defies
this intuition — it carries a *large* dependency depth (its *weight*) while
still admitting a *small* proof complexity.  In other words it floats: maximal
weight, minimal proof cost.

We model the one-way-function (OWF) level of the hierarchy as the type
`OWFStratum`, whose points are the OWF-level theorems indexed by their
dependency depth.  Two structural metrics are attached to each point:

* `OWFStratum.weight` — the **anti-gravity weight**, i.e. the dependency depth.
* `OWFStratum.proofComplexity` — the **proof complexity metric**, the number of
  irreducible (prime) reduction steps needed, i.e. `Ω(n)` counted with
  multiplicity.  This is exactly the metric used by `AntiGravity.proofCost`.

The hierarchy carries the **anti-gravity topology**: a set is open iff it is
*upper* with respect to weight (an Alexandrov upper-set topology generated by
dependency depth).  Concretely, once a theorem of a given weight is admitted,
all heavier theorems are too.

## Main results

* `OWFStratum.two_pow_proofComplexity_le` — the **anti-gravity trade-off**:
  `2 ^ proofComplexity n ≤ n`, so proof complexity is at most logarithmic in
  weight; high-weight theorems are forced to have low complexity.
* `OWFStratum.antiGravity_unbounded_weight` — anti-gravity theorems occur at
  arbitrarily large weight.
* `OWFStratum.antiGravity_dense` — the **density theorem**: anti-gravity
  theorems are dense in the anti-gravity topology on the OWF level.  Equivalently,
  every nonempty open family of OWF-level theorems contains an anti-gravity one.
* `OWFStratum.owf_greatest` — links the construction back to the hierarchy:
  OWF is the weakest (greatest, in the `≤`-of-`CryptoLevel` reverse order)
  primitive, so it is the natural level on which to study density.

The mathematical engine behind density is the **infinitude of primes**: prime
indices are precisely the theorems of minimal positive proof complexity, and
they are cofinal in weight.
-/

open Finset BigOperators

namespace AntiGravityWeight

/-! ## The OWF stratum and its two structural metrics -/

/-- The one-way-function level of the hardness hierarchy, presented as the space
of OWF-level theorems indexed by their dependency depth.  As a carrier it is `ℕ`,
but it is equipped with the anti-gravity (upper-set) topology below rather than
the usual order topology on `ℕ`. -/
def OWFStratum : Type := ℕ

namespace OWFStratum

instance : DecidableEq OWFStratum := inferInstanceAs (DecidableEq ℕ)
instance : Inhabited OWFStratum := inferInstanceAs (Inhabited ℕ)

/-- The **anti-gravity weight** of a theorem: its dependency depth. -/
def weight (n : OWFStratum) : ℕ := (n : ℕ)

/-- The **proof-complexity metric**: the number of irreducible reduction steps,
counted with multiplicity (`Ω(n)`).  This is the same metric as
`AntiGravity.proofCost`. -/
def proofComplexity (n : OWFStratum) : ℕ := (Nat.primeFactorsList (weight n)).length

@[simp] theorem weight_def (n : ℕ) : weight (n : OWFStratum) = n := rfl

@[simp] theorem proofComplexity_def (n : ℕ) :
    proofComplexity (n : OWFStratum) = (Nat.primeFactorsList n).length := rfl

/-! ## The anti-gravity topology (upper sets w.r.t. weight) -/

/-- The **anti-gravity topology**: a set of OWF-level theorems is open iff it is
closed upward under weight.  Once a theorem of some dependency depth is present,
every heavier theorem is present too. -/
instance instTopologicalSpace : TopologicalSpace OWFStratum where
  IsOpen S := ∀ n m : OWFStratum, n ∈ S → weight n ≤ weight m → m ∈ S
  isOpen_univ := by intro n m _ _; trivial
  isOpen_inter := by
    intro s t hs ht n m hn hnm
    exact ⟨hs n m hn.1 hnm, ht n m hn.2 hnm⟩
  isOpen_sUnion := by
    intro F hF n m hn hnm
    obtain ⟨s, hs, hns⟩ := hn
    exact ⟨s, hs, hF s hs n m hns hnm⟩

/-- Unfolding lemma: openness is exactly upward closure under weight. -/
theorem isOpen_iff_upper {S : Set OWFStratum} :
    IsOpen S ↔ ∀ n m : OWFStratum, n ∈ S → weight n ≤ weight m → m ∈ S :=
  Iff.rfl

/-! ## The anti-gravity trade-off and the anti-gravity predicate -/

/-- **Anti-gravity trade-off.**  For every positive dependency depth,
`2 ^ proofComplexity n ≤ n`: the proof-complexity metric is at most logarithmic
in the weight.  Thus a theorem of large weight is *forced* to have small
complexity — the quantitative core of the "anti-gravity" phenomenon. -/
theorem two_pow_proofComplexity_le {n : OWFStratum} (hn : 0 < weight n) :
    2 ^ proofComplexity n ≤ weight n := by
  have h : ∀ x ∈ (weight n).primeFactorsList, 2 ≤ x := fun x hx =>
    (Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactorsList hx).two_le
  have key : ∀ l : List ℕ, (∀ x ∈ l, 2 ≤ x) → 2 ^ l.length ≤ l.prod := by
    intro l
    induction l with
    | nil => simp
    | cons x xs ih =>
      intro hl
      have hx : 2 ≤ x := hl x List.mem_cons_self
      have htail : ∀ y ∈ xs, 2 ≤ y := fun y hy => hl y (List.mem_cons_of_mem x hy)
      have := ih htail
      simp only [List.length_cons, List.prod_cons, pow_succ]
      calc 2 ^ xs.length * 2 ≤ xs.prod * x := Nat.mul_le_mul this hx
        _ = x * xs.prod := by ring
  have hle := key (weight n).primeFactorsList h
  rwa [Nat.prod_primeFactorsList hn.ne'] at hle

/-- A theorem is an **anti-gravity theorem** when its proof complexity is minimal
(at most one irreducible reduction step, i.e. an irreducible/atomic theorem).
By `two_pow_proofComplexity_le` such theorems may nevertheless carry arbitrarily
large weight, which is exactly what `antiGravity_unbounded_weight` and
`antiGravity_dense` establish. -/
def IsAntiGravity (n : OWFStratum) : Prop := proofComplexity n ≤ 1

/-- Prime-indexed theorems are anti-gravity theorems: an irreducible reduction
step has proof complexity exactly one. -/
theorem isAntiGravity_of_prime {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) :
    IsAntiGravity (p : OWFStratum) := by
  simp [IsAntiGravity, proofComplexity, Nat.primeFactorsList_prime hp]

/-! ## High weight at low complexity, and density on the OWF level -/

/-- **Anti-gravity theorems reach unbounded weight.**  For every weight floor `k`
there is an anti-gravity theorem of weight at least `k`: arbitrarily heavy
theorems still admit minimal proof complexity. -/
theorem antiGravity_unbounded_weight (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ n : OWFStratum, IsAntiGravity n ∧ k ≤ weight n := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hpp⟩ := Nat.exists_infinite_primes k
  exact ⟨(p : OWFStratum), isAntiGravity_of_prime hpp, hp⟩

/-- **Density theorem.**  Anti-gravity theorems are dense in the anti-gravity
topology on the OWF level: every nonempty open family of OWF-level theorems
contains an anti-gravity theorem.  The proof uses the infinitude of primes —
prime-indexed (irreducible) theorems are cofinal in weight, and openness is
upward closure under weight. -/
theorem antiGravity_dense : Dense {n : OWFStratum | IsAntiGravity n} := by
  rw [dense_iff_inter_open]
  intro U hU hne
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := hne
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hpp⟩ := Nat.exists_infinite_primes (weight n)
  refine ⟨(p : OWFStratum), hU n p hn ?_, isAntiGravity_of_prime hpp⟩
  simpa [weight] using hp

/-! ## Link back to the hardness hierarchy -/

* `cut_submodular`            — the cut function is submodular (the structural heart of RT).
* `entropy_subadditive`       — `S(A ∪ A') ≤ S(A) + S(A')`  (subadditivity).
* `entropy_strong_subadditive`— `S(AB) + S(BC) ≥ S(ABC) + S(B)`  (strong subadditivity, SSA).
* `entropy_purity`            — for a symmetric (undirected) network, `S(A) = S(Dᶜ-in-D of A)`

* EXPERIMENT.  Per-edge submodularity was first verified by exhaustive case split on the four

namespace TensorNetworkSpacetime

open Finset

variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V]

/-- The (directed) **cut weight** of a vertex set `S`: the number of edges of the network `E`
that leave `S` (tail in `S`, head outside `S`).  In the large bond-dimension limit this is the
entanglement entropy contributed by the cut, in units of `log(bond dimension)`. -/
def cut (E : Finset (V × V)) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ e ∈ E, (if e.1 ∈ S ∧ e.2 ∉ S then 1 else 0)

/-- **Submodularity of the cut function** — the structural heart of the Ryu–Takayanagi
formula.  Proven from a per-edge Boolean inequality summed over the network. -/
theorem cut_submodular (E : Finset (V × V)) (S T : Finset V) :
    cut E (S ∪ T) + cut E (S ∩ T) ≤ cut E S + cut E T := by
  unfold cut
  rw [← Finset.sum_add_distrib, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_le_sum
  intro e _
  obtain ⟨a, b⟩ := e
  simp only [mem_union, mem_inter]
  by_cases h1 : a ∈ S <;> by_cases h2 : a ∈ T <;> by_cases h3 : b ∈ S <;> by_cases h4 : b ∈ T <;>
    simp_all

/-- The empty wedge has zero cut. -/
theorem cut_empty (E : Finset (V × V)) : cut E ∅ = 0 := by simp [cut]

/-- Every cut is bounded by the total number of edges (a discrete "area law" ceiling). -/
theorem cut_le_card (E : Finset (V × V)) (S : Finset V) : cut E S ≤ E.card := by
  unfold cut
  calc ∑ e ∈ E, (if e.1 ∈ S ∧ e.2 ∉ S then 1 else 0)
      ≤ ∑ _e ∈ E, 1 := by apply Finset.sum_le_sum; intro e _; split <;> simp
    _ = E.card := by simp

/-- **Holographic entanglement entropy** of a boundary region `A` (with respect to boundary
`B`): the minimal cut weight over all entanglement wedges `W` (vertex sets with `W ∩ B = A`).
This is the discrete Ryu–Takayanagi prescription. -/
noncomputable def entropy (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n | ∃ W : Finset V, W ∩ B = A ∧ cut E W = n}

/-- The entropy is at most the cut of any admissible wedge. -/
theorem entropy_le_of_wedge (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A W : Finset V)
    (hW : W ∩ B = A) : entropy E B A ≤ cut E W :=
  Nat.sInf_le ⟨W, hW, rfl⟩

/-- The minimum defining the entropy is attained: there is an optimal wedge. -/
theorem exists_wedge_eq_entropy (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A : Finset V) (hAB : A ⊆ B) :
    ∃ W : Finset V, W ∩ B = A ∧ cut E W = entropy E B A := by
  have hne : {n | ∃ W : Finset V, W ∩ B = A ∧ cut E W = n}.Nonempty :=
    ⟨cut E A, A, inter_eq_left.mpr hAB, rfl⟩
  obtain ⟨W, hW, hWcut⟩ := Nat.sInf_mem hne
  exact ⟨W, hW, hWcut⟩

/-- The empty region carries no entropy. -/
theorem entropy_empty (E : Finset (V × V)) (B : Finset V) : entropy E B ∅ = 0 := by
  have : entropy E B ∅ ≤ cut E ∅ := entropy_le_of_wedge E B ∅ ∅ (by simp)
  simpa [cut_empty] using this

/-- The region's own cut is an upper bound for its entropy. -/
theorem entropy_le_cut (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A : Finset V) (hAB : A ⊆ B) :
    entropy E B A ≤ cut E A :=
  entropy_le_of_wedge E B A A (inter_eq_left.mpr hAB)

/-- Discrete area-law ceiling: entropy never exceeds the total edge count. -/
theorem entropy_le_card (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A : Finset V) (hAB : A ⊆ B) :
    entropy E B A ≤ E.card :=
  le_trans (entropy_le_cut E B A hAB) (cut_le_card E A)

/-- **Subadditivity** of holographic entropy: `S(A ∪ A') ≤ S(A) + S(A')`.
Glue the optimal wedges of `A` and `A'` by union and apply submodularity. -/
theorem entropy_subadditive (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A A' : Finset V)
    (hA : A ⊆ B) (hA' : A' ⊆ B) :
    entropy E B (A ∪ A') ≤ entropy E B A + entropy E B A' := by
  obtain ⟨X, hX, hXc⟩ := exists_wedge_eq_entropy E B A hA
  obtain ⟨Y, hY, hYc⟩ := exists_wedge_eq_entropy E B A' hA'
  have hwedge : (X ∪ Y) ∩ B = A ∪ A' := by
    rw [Finset.union_inter_distrib_right, hX, hY]
  calc entropy E B (A ∪ A') ≤ cut E (X ∪ Y) := entropy_le_of_wedge E B (A ∪ A') (X ∪ Y) hwedge
    _ ≤ cut E (X ∪ Y) + cut E (X ∩ Y) := Nat.le_add_right _ _
    _ ≤ cut E X + cut E Y := cut_submodular E X Y
    _ = entropy E B A + entropy E B A' := by rw [hXc, hYc]

/-- Set identity used in SSA: for `Disjoint A C`, `(A ∪ B) ∩ (B ∪ C) = B`. -/
theorem inter_union_inter (A B C : Finset V) (hAC : Disjoint A C) :
    (A ∪ B) ∩ (B ∪ C) = B := by
  ext x
  simp only [mem_inter, mem_union]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hL, hR⟩
    rcases hL with hA | hB
    · rcases hR with hB | hC
      · exact hB
      · exact absurd hC (Finset.disjoint_left.mp hAC hA)
    · exact hB
  · intro hB; exact ⟨Or.inr hB, Or.inl hB⟩

/-- **Strong subadditivity** (SSA): `S(AB) + S(BC) ≥ S(ABC) + S(B)`.
Take optimal wedges `X` for `A∪B` and `Y` for `B∪C`; then `X∪Y` is a wedge for `A∪B∪C`,
`X∩Y` is a wedge for `B`, and submodularity closes the gap. -/
theorem entropy_strong_subadditive (E : Finset (V × V)) (D A B C : Finset V)
    (hA : A ⊆ D) (hB : B ⊆ D) (hC : C ⊆ D) (hAC : Disjoint A C) :
    entropy E D (A ∪ B ∪ C) + entropy E D B
      ≤ entropy E D (A ∪ B) + entropy E D (B ∪ C) := by
  obtain ⟨X, hX, hXc⟩ := exists_wedge_eq_entropy E D (A ∪ B) (union_subset hA hB)
  obtain ⟨Y, hY, hYc⟩ := exists_wedge_eq_entropy E D (B ∪ C) (union_subset hB hC)
  have hABC : (X ∪ Y) ∩ D = A ∪ B ∪ C := by
    rw [Finset.union_inter_distrib_right, hX, hY]
    ext x; simp only [mem_union]; tauto
  have hBwedge : (X ∩ Y) ∩ D = B := by
    rw [Finset.inter_inter_distrib_right, hX, hY]
    exact inter_union_inter A B C hAC
  calc entropy E D (A ∪ B ∪ C) + entropy E D B
      ≤ cut E (X ∪ Y) + cut E (X ∩ Y) :=
        Nat.add_le_add (entropy_le_of_wedge E D (A ∪ B ∪ C) (X ∪ Y) hABC)
          (entropy_le_of_wedge E D B (X ∩ Y) hBwedge)
    _ ≤ cut E X + cut E Y := cut_submodular E X Y
    _ = entropy E D (A ∪ B) + entropy E D (B ∪ C) := by rw [hXc, hYc]

/-! ### Mutual information and emergent connectivity -/

/-- Discrete **mutual information** `I(A:A') = S(A) + S(A') - S(A∪A')` (truncated ℕ subtraction). -/
noncomputable def mutualInfo (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A A' : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  entropy E B A + entropy E B A' - entropy E B (A ∪ A')

/-- Mutual information is realized exactly (no ℕ truncation), because of subadditivity:
`I(A:A') + S(A∪A') = S(A) + S(A')`.  In particular `I(A:A') ≥ 0`, the discrete seed of
"shared entanglement glues regions together" (ER = EPR). -/
theorem mutualInfo_add_entropy_union (E : Finset (V × V)) (B A A' : Finset V)
    (hA : A ⊆ B) (hA' : A' ⊆ B) :
    mutualInfo E B A A' + entropy E B (A ∪ A') = entropy E B A + entropy E B A' := by
  unfold mutualInfo
  exact Nat.sub_add_cancel (entropy_subadditive E B A A' hA hA')

/-! ### Purity for symmetric (undirected) networks -/

/-- For a symmetric edge multiset, the directed cut is reflection-symmetric:
`cut E S = cut E Sᶜ`.  This is where "the global state is pure" enters. -/
theorem cut_symm [Fintype V] (E : Finset (V × V)) (hE : E.image Prod.swap = E) (S : Finset V) :
    cut E S = cut E Sᶜ := by
  unfold cut
  conv_rhs => rw [← hE]
  rw [Finset.sum_image (by intro a _ b _ h; exact Prod.swap_injective h)]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro e _
  obtain ⟨a, b⟩ := e
  simp only [Prod.swap, mem_compl]
  by_cases h1 : a ∈ S <;> by_cases h2 : b ∈ S <;> simp_all

/-- One direction of purity: `S(D \ A) ≤ S(A)` for a symmetric network. -/
theorem entropy_compl_le [Fintype V] (E : Finset (V × V)) (hE : E.image Prod.swap = E)
    (D A : Finset V) (hAD : A ⊆ D) : entropy E D (D \ A) ≤ entropy E D A := by
  obtain ⟨W, hW, hWc⟩ := exists_wedge_eq_entropy E D A hAD
  have hwedge : Wᶜ ∩ D = D \ A := by
    rw [← hW]; ext x; simp only [mem_inter, mem_compl, mem_sdiff]; tauto
  calc entropy E D (D \ A) ≤ cut E Wᶜ := entropy_le_of_wedge E D (D \ A) Wᶜ hwedge
    _ = cut E W := (cut_symm E hE W).symm
    _ = entropy E D A := hWc

/-- **Ryu–Takayanagi purity**: for a symmetric (undirected) tensor network — modelling a pure
global state — a boundary region and its complement carry equal entropy: `S(D \ A) = S(A)`. -/
theorem entropy_purity [Fintype V] (E : Finset (V × V)) (hE : E.image Prod.swap = E)
    (D A : Finset V) (hAD : A ⊆ D) : entropy E D (D \ A) = entropy E D A := by
  refine le_antisymm (entropy_compl_le E hE D A hAD) ?_
  have h2 := entropy_compl_le E hE D (D \ A) (sdiff_subset)
  rwa [sdiff_sdiff_eq_self hAD] at h2

/-- **Araki–Lieb (triangle) inequality** for a symmetric (pure) network:
`S(A) ≤ S(B) + S(A ∪ B)`.  Derived from purity together with subadditivity applied to the
complement `D \ A = B ∪ (D \ (A ∪ B))`.  By symmetry in `A, B` this gives the full
`|S(A) − S(B)| ≤ S(A ∪ B)`. -/
theorem entropy_araki_lieb [Fintype V] (E : Finset (V × V)) (hE : E.image Prod.swap = E)
    (D A B : Finset V) (hA : A ⊆ D) (hB : B ⊆ D) (hAB : Disjoint A B) :
    entropy E D A ≤ entropy E D B + entropy E D (A ∪ B) := by
  have hABD : A ∪ B ⊆ D := union_subset hA hB
  have hset : B ∪ (D \ (A ∪ B)) = D \ A := by
    ext x; simp only [mem_union, mem_sdiff]
    constructor
    · rintro (hxB | ⟨hxD, hxAB⟩)
      · exact ⟨hB hxB, fun hxA => (Finset.disjoint_left.mp hAB hxA) hxB⟩
      · exact ⟨hxD, fun hxA => hxAB (Or.inl hxA)⟩
    · rintro ⟨hxD, hxA⟩
      by_cases hxB : x ∈ B
      · exact Or.inl hxB
      · exact Or.inr ⟨hxD, by simp [hxA, hxB]⟩
  have hsub : entropy E D (D \ A) ≤ entropy E D B + entropy E D (D \ (A ∪ B)) := by
    rw [← hset]
    exact entropy_subadditive E D B (D \ (A ∪ B)) hB sdiff_subset
  rwa [entropy_purity E hE D A hA, entropy_purity E hE D (A ∪ B) hABD] at hsub

/-! ### Emergent metric geometry from the same network

The undirected graph underlying the network induces a graph distance.  We record that this
distance is an emergent pseudometric (symmetric, vanishing on the diagonal, triangle
inequality on each connected component), i.e. *spacetime distance emerges from the network*. -/

/-- The undirected graph generated by the network's edge multiset. -/
noncomputable def networkGraph (E : Finset (V × V)) : SimpleGraph V :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun u v => (u, v) ∈ E)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- Emergent distance vanishes on the diagonal. -/
theorem emergent_dist_self (E : Finset (V × V)) (v : V) :
    (networkGraph E).dist v v = 0 := SimpleGraph.dist_self

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- Emergent distance is symmetric. -/
theorem emergent_dist_comm (E : Finset (V × V)) (u v : V) :
    (networkGraph E).dist u v = (networkGraph E).dist v u := SimpleGraph.dist_comm

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- Emergent distance obeys the triangle inequality on a connected network. -/
theorem emergent_dist_triangle (E : Finset (V × V)) (h : (networkGraph E).Connected)
    (u v w : V) :
    (networkGraph E).dist u w ≤ (networkGraph E).dist u v + (networkGraph E).dist v w :=
  h.dist_triangle

end TensorNetworkSpacetime
